I have somewhat different view than most having cut my options teeth on a dispersion book during the tech bubble.  

The index vol short half of the short correlation trade was always a choice in terms of its sizing.  Back then IV/RV premium was pretty narrow unlike today so every unit of Vega sold in index was managed carefully.  Being short index vol was a coin flip sort of trade.   The sizing ranged from Vega neutral to single stock book (which collected theta) to theta neutral which was Vega long. 

The drop in implied correlation makes the trade less attractive.  But given the level of implied on index the notable risk isn't selling index vol to low its buying single name vol way way too high.  The root causes of that single name vol levels are numerous including speculative demand and the dispersion trader competing to buy elevated single name vol.  the seller is absent and gets a sweet risk premium when providing any liquidity. The risk the dispersionis at most risk to is a single name vol  collapse.  Perhaps a large equity drawdown would also be a negative single name vol event but that seems pretty unlikely.  So then it comes down to hedging index level and sizing.  

Is the CIO buying index puts to hedge the dispersion traders?  Jeez maybe but then the LP's are just long single name vol at extremely elevated levels.  

My picture is of course if macro drives index levels down index implied will get bid up but on the day so will single name vol.  

Frankly the responsible CIO would be finding ways to get short single name vol if they are really worried NOT buying index puts at 20+ vol

But mostly I don't see them hedging much at all

Brent just printed $118 and the 10-year Treasury yield is at 4.94%. That relationship used to run the other way .

@robin_j_brooks is correct in this analysis. This is a regime shift, not a blip.

For most of 2026, oil up meant yields up. Inflation expectations fed straight into the long end. That link is now broken. The 20-day correlation between Brent and the 10Y has collapsed to its lowest since late 2024.

The reason is Europe. The French 10-year is at 4.96%, the highest since 2002. The spread over German Bunds has widened to 159bp, the widest since 2011. French debt-to-GDP is 117%, versus 90% at the last crisis peak.

Bessent confirmed this week that capital is leaving "concerning" jurisdictions and flowing into Treasuries as a safe haven. The US is catching a bid because the alternative is worse.

This is not a resolution of the fiscal problem. Net interest is still above $1 trillion. The term premium is being temporarily suppressed by a flight to quality, not by better US math.

If Europe stabilizes, the bid fades. If Europe cracks, the bid deepens.

Chamath: The AI Boom Has a Borrowing Problem

“The entire United States economy is levered to the AI complex.

So very narrowly, we're talking about seven or eight companies that set the tone for the entire country. And whether we like it or not, that is where we are.

Why do I say that? The most important companies in the world are in a massive spending binge, right?

These were highly profitable, highly cash accretive, highly cash flow generative businesses that have said, ‘We're going to put the foot down on spending because we believe in what's coming into the future.’ That's what drives GDP and it's what drives growth.

Now, as they do that though, they deplete their cash and they have to raise debt.

The AI complex now owes $340-400 billion to the market. And you'd say, ‘Okay, why is that important?’

The problem is this: These companies are raising so much money it starts to crowd out the capital markets.

And the most important part of the capital market that it starts to crowd out, is the appetite for government treasuries.

And what you can see here is that when you look at these AI firms, the amount of money that they need to raise through the end of '27, it's 30% of all of what the Treasury's about to issue in that same period.

So, whether we like it or not, they are going to start competing for demand.”
